School

Stoicism quotes

Stoicism is a Hellenistic school teaching that living in agreement with nature and reason—through virtue—is the path to a flourishing life.

35 passages · 4 voices in this archive selection

Overview

Founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens around 300 BCE, Stoicism divides philosophy into physics, logic, and ethics. Virtue is the only true good; externals such as wealth, health, and reputation are preferred or dispreferred indifferents. Passions are understood as mistaken judgments; the sage’s ideal is rational consistency, while progressors practice daily discipline.

Historical notes

Early Stoics (Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus) built a systematic school; Roman writers—Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius—preserve the most complete surviving ethical works. Modern readers often meet Stoicism as practical counsel, but classical Stoicism also included logic and a providential physics.

Core ideas

  • Virtue is necessary and sufficient for happiness.
  • Some things are up to us (judgment, impulse); others are not.
  • Live according to nature—human nature as rational and social.
  • Practice: examine impressions before assenting to them.

Thinkers in this archive

Epictetus , Seneca , Marcus Aurelius , Cicero

FAQ

What is Stoicism in simple terms?

Stoicism teaches that a good life centers on virtue and wise judgment, not on controlling external events.

Who are the main Stoic philosophers?

Early founders include Zeno and Chrysippus; the most-read Roman Stoics are Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius.
